By now I was top of the school of rhetoric, and I was proud and pleased with myself and swollen with conceit, though (Lord, you know) far quieter than, and entirely apart from, the wreckings of those self-styled "Wreckers" — for that grim and devilish name was their badge of sophistication — among whom I lived in a kind of shameless shame at not being one of them. I lived among them, and sometimes I enjoyed their company, while I always loathed what they did: their "wreckings," the way they would wantonly hound the modesty of newcomers, throwing them off balance with pointless mockery, feeding their own malice on it. Nothing is more like the very work of demons than this. What truer name could they be given than "Wreckers"? — themselves first of all wrecked and utterly twisted, with the deceiving spirits secretly laughing at them and luring them on, in the very act of luring and laughing at others.

Living among people like that, at that unsteady age, I studied books of eloquence, in which I longed to shine — for a damnable, empty-headed reason: delight in human vanity. In the ordinary course of study I came upon a book by a certain Cicero, whose tongue almost everyone admires, though not his heart. This particular book of his is an exhortation to philosophy, and it is called the Hortensius. That book changed how I felt. It turned my prayers toward you, Lord, and gave me new purposes and longings. Suddenly every empty hope looked worthless to me, and with an unbelievable fire in my heart I began to long for the immortality that wisdom is, and I began to get up and start back toward you. For it was not to sharpen my tongue that I used that book — sharpening my tongue was what I seemed to be buying with my mother's money, in that nineteenth year of mine, my father having died two years before — it was not for its style that I read it, but for what it said.

How I burned then, my God, how I burned to fly up from earthly things back to you, and I had no idea what you were going to do with me. For with you is wisdom. And love of wisdom is what the Greek word "philosophy" means, and it was with this love that the book set me ablaze. There are people who use philosophy to lead others astray, dressing up their own errors under that great, smooth, respectable name — and almost everyone who did so in that age and earlier ages is named and exposed in that book. There, too, stands out that healthy warning given by your Spirit through your good and devoted servant: See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, following human tradition and the elementary principles of the world, and not Christ; for in him the whole fullness of God dwells in bodily form. And since at that time (you, the light of my heart, know it) I had no knowledge of the apostolic Scriptures, this is all the exhortation delighted me to do: it roused and kindled and inflamed me to love and seek and win and hold and embrace not this or that school of thought, but wisdom itself, whatever it might be. One thing alone held back my blaze: that the name of Christ was not in it. For this name, by your mercy, Lord, this name of my Savior, your Son, my tender heart had drunk in devoutly with my mother's milk and stored away deep — and whatever lacked that name, however learned and polished and true, could never take complete hold of me.

So I made up my mind to turn to the holy Scriptures and see what they were like. But look — here was something the proud cannot grasp and yet is not laid bare to children; lowly to enter, but in its depths towering, and veiled in mystery. And I was not the kind of person who could enter into it, or bend my neck to walk its path. For I did not feel about those Scriptures, when I first turned to them, what I am saying now. They struck me as unworthy to be set beside the grandeur of Cicero. My swollen pride recoiled from their plainness, and my sharp wit could not pierce to their inner meaning. Yet they were exactly the kind of thing that grows along with a little child. But I scorned to be a little child, and, puffed up with pride, I took myself for someone great.

So I fell in with men full of proud nonsense, utterly carnal and talkative, in whose mouths were the snares of the Devil — birdlime smeared together out of the syllables of your name, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, our Comforter. These names never left their mouths, but only as sound, as the noise of the tongue; their hearts were empty of truth. And still they kept crying "Truth! Truth!" and saying much about it to me, and it was never in them. They spoke falsehood not only about you, who truly are the Truth, but even about these elements of the world, your creatures. And I should have walked right past even the philosophers who spoke truth about such things, for love of you, my Father, supreme good, Beauty of all things beautiful. O Truth, Truth, how deeply even then the marrow of my soul ached for you, while these men kept dinning your name in my ears, again and again, in many ways, in many huge books — and it was only an echo. And these were the dishes on which, while I starved for you, they served me up the sun and moon instead of you — beautiful works of yours, yes, but works, not you, and not even your first works. For your spiritual works come before these physical ones, splendid and shining though they are. But I hungered and thirsted not even for those first works of yours; I hungered for you yourself, the Truth, in whom there is no change, not even the shadow of turning. And still they set before me in those dishes their glittering fantasies, when it would have been better to love this very sun, which is at least real to our eyes, than those fantasies that deceive the mind through the eyes. Yet because I thought they were you, I fed on them — not eagerly, for in them you did not taste to me as you really are. You were not those empty things, and I was not nourished by them; I was drained instead. Food in a dream looks just like food when we are awake, yet sleepers are not fed by it, for they are asleep. But those fantasies were not even like you in the way you have now spoken to me; for they were bodily fantasies, false bodies — and the real bodies we see with our eyes of flesh, in the sky or on the earth, are far more certain than they. The beasts and birds see these real bodies as well as we do, and they are more certain than the bodies we merely imagine; and the ones we imagine are in turn more certain than the vaster, endless bodies we go on to guess at from them, which have no existence at all. On such empty husks I was being fed in those days, and not fed. But you, the Love of my soul, in seeking whom I grow weak so that I may grow strong, you are not those bodies we see, even up in heaven, nor the ones we do not see there; for you made them, and you do not even count them among your highest works. How far, then, you are from those fantasies of mine, fantasies of bodies that do not exist at all — when the images of bodies that do exist are far more certain than my fantasies, and the bodies themselves more certain still, which yet you are not; nor are you even the soul, which is the life of bodies. So the life of bodies is better and more certain than the bodies. But you are the life of souls, the life of lives, alive in yourself, and you do not change, O life of my soul.

Where, then, were you to me in those days, and how far off? Far indeed I was wandering from you, shut out even from the husks of the pigs I was feeding with husks. For how much better are the stories of poets and grammar-teachers than these snares of theirs? Verses and poems and "Medea taking flight" are honestly more useful than these men's five elements painted in different disguises, answering to five dens of darkness — things that have no existence, yet kill whoever believes in them. Verses and poems I can turn into real food; and though I once recited "Medea taking flight," I never claimed it was true, and though I heard it recited, I never believed it — but those Manichaean things I did believe. What a pity, what a pity, by what steps I was led down into the depths of hell, sweating and straining for lack of Truth — for I was seeking you, my God (to you I confess it, you who had mercy on me even before I confessed), not with the understanding of the mind, by which you meant me to surpass the beasts, but with the sense of the flesh. But you were more inward to me than my innermost self, and higher than the highest in me. I stumbled upon that brazen woman, foolish and knowing nothing, sketched in Solomon's proverb, sitting at her door and saying, Eat the bread of secrecy gladly, and drink the sweet stolen waters. She seduced me, because she found my soul living outside itself, in the eye of my flesh, chewing over the food I had swallowed through it.

For I knew nothing else than this — than what really is I had no knowledge — and I was talked into agreeing, as though by sheer cleverness, with stupid deceivers when they asked me: "Where does evil come from?" "Is God bounded by a bodily shape, with hair and nails?" "Are men to be counted righteous who had many wives at once, and killed men, and sacrificed living animals?" At all this I, in my ignorance, was badly shaken, and while moving away from the truth I imagined I was moving toward it — because I did not yet know that evil is nothing but a lack of good, right down to the point where a thing ceases to exist at all. And how was I to see this, when the sight of my eyes reached only as far as bodies, and the sight of my mind only as far as a phantom? I did not know that God is Spirit, with no parts stretched out in length and breadth, no being that is sheer bulk — for every bulk is less in a part than in the whole, and if it were infinite it would be less in any part marked off by a given space than in its whole infinity, and so could not be wholly everywhere, as Spirit is, as God is. And as for what it is in us by which we resemble God, so that we can rightly be called made in the image of God, I had no idea at all.

Nor did I know that true, inward righteousness which judges not by custom but out of the perfectly right law of God Almighty — the law by which the moral ways of different places and times were each fitted to their own time and place, while the law itself stays one and the same always and everywhere, not one thing here and another there. By this righteousness Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and Moses and David were righteous, and all those praised by the mouth of God, even though shallow men, judging by human judgment and measuring the moral practice of the whole human race by their own narrow habits, counted them unrighteous. It is as if someone who knew nothing about armor, ignorant of which piece fits which part of the body, were to put the leg-guards on his head and try to wear the helmet on his feet, and then complain that they did not fit. Or as if, on a day when business is shut down for the afternoon, a man were furious at not being allowed to keep his shop open, just because he had been allowed to in the morning. Or as if, in one household, he saw a servant handle something the wine-steward is not permitted to touch, or saw something allowed out in the yard that is forbidden at the dinner table, and grew angry that within one house and one family the same thing is not allowed everywhere and to everyone. Such are the people who fume to hear that something was lawful for righteous men long ago which is not lawful now, or that God for certain temporal reasons commanded those men one thing and these men another, while both obeyed one and the same righteousness — when in a single body, a single day, a single household, they plainly see different things fitting for different parts, and a thing once lawful unlawful a little later, permitted or commanded in one corner but rightly forbidden and punished in another. Is justice, then, changeable and inconsistent? No — but the times it presides over do not run all alike, precisely because they are times. Men, though, whose days on earth are few, cannot piece together by their senses how the causes of things in earlier ages and other nations, which they have no experience of, fit with the causes they do have experience of; and so, while in one body or day or family they easily see what suits each part and season and person, they take offense at the one and submit to the other.

These things I did not yet know or notice. They struck my eyes on every side and I did not see them. When I composed verses, I could not put just any metrical foot just anywhere; I had to place them differently in different meters, and even within a single meter I could not put the same foot in every position. Yet the art of poetry itself, by which I composed, did not have different principles for these different cases; it held them all in one. And still I could not see how that righteousness which good and holy men obeyed contained, far more excellently and loftily, in one single principle, all the things God commanded, never varying in any part — even though in varying times it did not prescribe everything at once, but assigned to each its own. And I, in my blindness, condemned the holy fathers, not only where they used the things of their own time as God commanded and inspired them, but even where they were foretelling things to come, as God was revealing them through them.

Can it ever, anywhere, be wrong to love God with all your heart and all your soul and all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself? And so those foul offenses against nature are everywhere and always to be detested and punished, such as the offenses of the men of Sodom; if every nation committed them, they would all stand guilty of the same crime under the law of God, which did not make human beings to abuse one another like that. For even the fellowship that ought to exist between God and us is violated when the very nature he authored is polluted by twisted lust. But offenses against the customs of men are to be avoided according to whatever customs are in force; so that what has been agreed and confirmed by the custom or law of any city or nation is not to be broken at the lawless whim of anyone, whether citizen or foreigner. For any part that does not fit with its whole is offensive. But when God commands a thing against the customs or agreements of any people, even something never done among them before, it is to be done; and if it has lapsed, it is to be restored; and if it was never established, it is now to be established. For if a king is allowed, in the realm he rules, to command something neither he nor anyone before him had ever commanded, and obeying him is not against the common good of the state — indeed it would be against it not to obey, since obedience to rulers is a general compact of human society — how much more unhesitatingly ought we to obey God, the Ruler of all his creatures, in everything he commands? For just as, among the powers in human society, the greater authority is obeyed in preference to the lesser, so must God be obeyed above all.

So too with acts of violence, where there is a wish to do harm, whether by insult or injury: done either for revenge, as one enemy against another; or for some gain belonging to someone else, as a robber against a traveler; or to escape some evil, as against a man one fears; or out of envy, as the less fortunate against the more fortunate, or a man doing well in some area against another whose mere equality he fears or resents; or for the sheer pleasure of another's pain, like the spectators at the gladiators, or the mockers and sneerers at other people. These are the chief headings of sin, and they spring from the lust of the flesh, or of the eye, or of power — singly, or two combined, or all three together. And so men live badly against the three, and the seven, that ten-stringed harp, your Ten Commandments, O God, most high and most sweet. But what foul offenses can there be against you, who cannot be defiled? What acts of violence against you, who cannot be harmed? What you avenge is what men commit against themselves, for even when they sin against you they are doing wickedness against their own souls, and their wrongdoing gives itself the lie — by corrupting and perverting the nature you created and ordered, whether through an excessive use of what is allowed, or by burning, in things not allowed, with a use against nature; or they are found guilty of raging with heart and tongue against you, kicking against the goads; or, bursting through the bounds of human fellowship, they brazenly delight in self-willed alliances or splits, depending on what they hope to gain or take offense at. And all this is done when you are forsaken, O Fountain of Life, the one true Maker and Ruler of the whole universe, and by self-willed pride some single false thing is picked out and loved. So it is by a humble devotion that we come back to you; you cleanse us of our bad habits, you are merciful to the sins of those who confess, you hear the groaning of the prisoner and free us from the chains we forged for ourselves — provided we do not raise against you the horns of a counterfeit freedom, losing everything through greed for more, by loving our own private good more than you, the Good of all.

In among these offenses of foulness and violence, these many wrongs, there are the sins of men who, on the whole, are making progress — sins which those who judge rightly, by the standard of perfection, disapprove of, while still commending the persons, in hope of future fruit, as in the green blade of growing grain. And there are some acts that look like offenses of foulness or violence and yet are not sins, because they wrong neither you, our Lord God, nor human society: as when something fitting for a particular moment is acquired for the service of life — and we cannot tell whether out of a craving to possess; or when something is punished, for the sake of correction, by lawful authority — and we cannot tell whether out of a craving to do harm. So many an action disapproved of in men's eyes is, by your testimony, approved; and many an action praised by men is, with you as witness, condemned — because the look of the deed, and the mind of the doer, and the hidden need of the moment, each vary. But when you suddenly command some unaccustomed, unthought-of thing — yes, even something you once forbade, and even while you keep the reason for your command hidden for a time, and even though it goes against the agreement of some human society — who can doubt that it is to be done, since a human society is only just when it serves you? But blessed are those who know your commands! For all the things your servants did were done either to display something needed for the present, or to foreshadow things to come.

Ignorant of all this, I mocked those holy servants and prophets of yours. And what did I gain by mocking them, except to be mocked by you, as I was insensibly drawn on, step by step, into such follies as believing that a fig tree weeps when its fruit is picked, that the tree, its mother, sheds milky tears? And yet, if some Manichaean "saint" had eaten that fig — picked by another man's sin, not his own — and digested it, he would breathe out angels from it; indeed, particles of divinity would burst out at every groan and sigh of his prayer, particles of the most high and true God that would have stayed trapped in that fig if they had not been set free by the teeth and belly of some "Elect" one. And I, poor fool, believed that more mercy was owed to the fruits of the earth than to the human beings they were created for. For if some hungry man who was not a Manichaean had asked for one, that mouthful would have been treated as good as condemned to death the moment it was handed over to him.

And you reached down your hand from above and drew my soul out of that deep darkness, while my mother, your faithful one, wept to you for me more than mothers weep over the bodily death of their children. For by the faith and the spirit she had from you, she saw the death I was lying in; and you heard her, O Lord. You heard her, and you did not despise her tears, when they streamed down and watered the ground beneath her eyes in every place where she prayed. Yes, you heard her. For where else did that dream come from, by which you comforted her, so that she agreed to live with me and to share the same table at home — something she had begun to refuse, shrinking back in horror and disgust from the blasphemies of my error? In the dream she saw herself standing on a wooden plank, and a young man coming toward her, radiant, cheerful, smiling at her, while she herself was grieving and crushed with grief. He asked her the reasons for her sorrow and her daily tears — asking, as such messengers do, in order to teach, not to be taught — and when she answered that she was mourning my ruin, he told her to be at peace, and bade her look and see "that where she was, there I was too." And when she looked, she saw me standing beside her on the same plank. Where did this come from, but that your ears were turned toward her heart, O Good and Almighty, who care for each one of us as if you cared for him alone, and for all as if each were the only one?

And where did this come from, too: that when she had told me the vision, and I tried to twist it to mean that she should not despair of one day becoming what I was, she answered at once, without a moment's hesitation: "No. I was not told, 'where he is, there you will be,' but 'where you are, there he will be'"? I confess to you, Lord, that as far as I can remember — and I have often spoken of this — your answer through my waking mother moved me more than the dream itself: that she was not thrown off by the plausibility of my false reading, and so quickly saw what was there to be seen, which I certainly had not seen before she spoke. By that dream a joy was promised to a holy woman long before it came true, to console her in her present anguish; for almost nine years were still to pass in which I wallowed in the mud of that deep pit and the darkness of falsehood, often trying to rise and being slammed down all the harder. All that time, that chaste, devout, level-headed widow — the kind you love — now more cheered with hope but no less steady in her weeping and mourning, never stopped pleading your case for me to you at every hour of her prayers. And her prayers reached your presence, and still you let me go on rolling and re-rolling in that darkness.

Meanwhile you gave her another answer, which I remember — for I am passing over much, hurrying on to the things that press me harder to confess to you, and much I do not remember. You gave her, then, another answer, through a priest of yours, a certain bishop raised in your Church and well-read in your books. When this woman begged him to be so good as to talk with me, refute my errors, unteach me what was bad, and teach me what was good — which he was in the habit of doing when he found people ready for it — he refused, wisely, as I later understood. For he answered that I was still unteachable, swollen with the novelty of that heresy, and that I had already tangled a number of unskilled people with my tricky questions, as she herself had told him. "But leave him alone for a while," he said. "Only pray to God for him. By his own reading he will discover what that error is, and how great its impiety." At the same time he told her how he himself, as a small boy, had been handed over to the Manichees by his own seduced mother, and had not only read but copied out almost all their books, and had come to see — without anyone arguing or proving it to him — how thoroughly that sect was to be shunned, and had shunned it. But when he had said this and she still would not be satisfied, pressing him harder with her pleading and her many tears to see me and have it out with me, he grew a little impatient with her insistence and said: "Go your way, and God bless you. It cannot be that the son of these tears should perish." And she took this answer, as she often told me later in our talks together, as though it had sounded from heaven.

For nine years — from my nineteenth year to my twenty-eighth — we lived seduced and seducing, deceived and deceiving, in every kind of lust. Openly, by way of the studies they call liberal; in secret, under the cover of a religion that lied about its own name. On the one side proud, on the other superstitious, and on every side empty. On the one side, chasing the emptiness of popular acclaim, right down to the applause of the theater, the prizes for poems, the contests for crowns of grass, the foolishness of the shows, the runaway appetites. On the other side, hoping to be cleansed of these very stains by carrying food to those who were called the "elect" and the "holy," so that in the workshop of their stomachs they might forge for us the angels and gods who were to cleanse us. These were the things I went after, and practiced with my friends — friends deceived by me, and along with me. Let the arrogant laugh at me, and all who have never yet been struck down and laid low by you, my God, for the saving of their souls; still I will confess to you my own shame, to your praise. Bear with me, I beg you, and give me grace to go back over the wanderings of my past life in my present memory, and to offer you the sacrifice of thanksgiving. For what am I to myself without you, but a guide steering my own way to ruin? Or what am I even at my best, but an infant sucking the milk you give, feeding on you, the food that does not perish? And what is any man, seeing he is only a man? Let the strong and the mighty laugh at us; let us, poor and needy, confess to you.

In those years I taught rhetoric, and, beaten down by greed, I put up for sale a skill in speech meant for beating others down. Yet I preferred — you know it, Lord — honest students, or those reckoned honest; and these, without any trickery, I taught the tricks of the trade, not to be used against the life of an innocent man, though sometimes to be used for the life of a guilty one. And you, God, watched me from far off, stumbling along that slippery road, and out of all that smoke sending up a few sparks of good faith, which I showed in guiding those who loved vanity and went looking for lies — I, their companion in it. In those years I had a woman, not one joined to me in what is called lawful marriage, but one my reckless and unthinking passion had hunted out. Yet she was the only one, and I stayed faithful even to her; and in her I learned for myself the difference between the restraint of the marriage covenant, entered into for the sake of children, and the bargain of a lustful love, where children are born against their parents' will — though, once born, they force you to love them.

I remember, too, that when I had decided to compete for a prize in the theater, some sorcerer asked me what I would pay him to win. But I loathed and shrank from those foul rites, and I answered that even if the crown were of imperishable gold, I would not let a single fly be killed to win it for me. For he was to slaughter living creatures in his sacrifices, and by those offerings to invite the demons to favor me. But even this evil I refused, and not out of any pure love for you, God of my heart — for I did not know how to love you, I who could conceive of nothing beyond a brightness of the body. And does not a soul that sighs after such fictions commit adultery against you, trust in things that are not real, and feed the wind? So I would not, it seems, have sacrifices offered to demons on my behalf — while by that very superstition I was sacrificing myself to them. For what is it to feed the wind, but to feed them — to become, by going astray, their pleasure and their sport?

So I went without scruple to consult those impostors they call astrologers, because they seemed to offer no sacrifice and to pray to no spirit for their fortune-telling — though true Christian devotion rightly rejects and condemns that art as well. For it is good to confess to you and to say, Have mercy on me, heal my soul, for I have sinned against you; and not to take your mercy as a license to sin, but to remember the Lord's words: See, you are made whole, sin no more, in case something worse should happen to you. All this saving counsel the astrologers labor to undo, when they say, "The cause of your sin is fixed beyond escape in the heavens," and "This was the work of Venus, or Saturn, or Mars" — so that a man, mere flesh and blood and rotting pride, should bear no blame, and the blame fall instead on the Maker and Orderer of heaven and the stars. And who is that but our God, the very sweetness and well-spring of righteousness, who pays back each man according to his deeds, and will not despise a broken and contrite heart?

In those days there was a wise man, very skilled and famous in medicine, who, in his office as proconsul, had with his own hand set the winner's crown on my disordered head — though not as a physician, for this sickness of mine is one that you alone can cure, you who resist the proud and give grace to the humble. And yet did you fail me even through that old man, or hold back from healing my soul? For I came to know him better, and hung steadily and closely on his words, which, though plainly spoken, were vivid and alive and earnest. When he gathered from my talk that I was given to the books of the horoscope-casters, he advised me, kindly, like a father, to throw them away, and not to waste on these empty things the care and effort that real and useful matters need. He told me that in his own early years he had studied that art with a mind to make it the trade he would live by; that since he had understood Hippocrates, he could easily have mastered this too — and yet he had given it up and turned to medicine, for no other reason than that he found it utterly false, and being a serious man, he would not earn his bread by fooling people. "But you," he said, "have rhetoric to support yourself by, so you follow this thing by free choice, not by need. All the more, then, should you take my word for it, since I worked to master it so thoroughly as to make my whole living from it." When I asked him how it was, then, that many true things were foretold by it, he gave me the best answer he could: that it was the power of chance, spread through the whole order of things, that brought this about. For if a man, opening at random the pages of some poet who had been singing and thinking of something else entirely, often lights on a verse that fits his present situation wonderfully well — it should be no wonder, he said, if out of the human soul, by some higher prompting it knows nothing of, an answer comes up, by luck and not by art, that matches the affairs and doings of the one who asks.

And so, either from him or through him, you conveyed this to me and traced it in my memory, for me to look into later for myself. But at that time neither he, nor my dearest Nebridius — a young man wholly good and full of holy reverence, who laughed at the whole business of divination — could talk me into casting it aside. The authority of the writers still swayed me more, and as yet I had found no sure proof, the kind I was looking for, that would show beyond all doubt that whatever those consultations foretold truly came about by chance and not by the stargazers' art.

In those years, when I first began to teach rhetoric in my home town, I had made a friend who was too dear to me — drawn together by a shared love of the same things — a man of my own age, and, like me, in the first opening flower of youth. He had grown up alongside me from childhood; we had gone to school together and played together. But he was not yet my friend in the way he later became, and even then it was not friendship in its truest sense; for true friendship cannot exist unless you bind it fast among those who cling to you, by the love poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who is given to us. Still, it was sweet to me, all too sweet, ripened in the warmth of shared studies. For I had turned him aside from the true faith — which, being young, he had not soundly and deeply taken in — and led him into those superstitious and ruinous fables over which my mother wept for me. With me he now wandered in his mind, and my soul could not be without him. But you were close behind your runaways, at once a God of vengeance and a fountain of mercy, turning us back to yourself by ways we could not have foreseen. You took that man out of this life when he had barely rounded out a single year of friendship with me — a friendship sweeter to me than all the sweetness of my whole life.

Who can tell all your praises that he has known in his own one self? What did you do then, my God, and how unsearchable is the deep abyss of your judgments? For he was long and gravely sick with a fever, and lay senseless in a death-sweat. When they gave up hope of his recovery, he was baptized while unconscious — and I gave it little thought, taking it for granted that his soul would hold on to what it had received from me rather than to what had been done to his unknowing body. But it turned out far otherwise. For he rallied and was restored to health; and the moment I could speak with him — which was as soon as he was able, since I never left his side, and we leaned on each other too heavily — I tried to make a joke of it, as though he would laugh with me at the baptism he had been given while utterly absent in mind and feeling, but which he had now learned that he had received. But he drew back from me as if I were an enemy, and with a sudden, astonishing independence he told me, as I valued his friendship, never to speak to him like that again. Dumbfounded and shaken, I held back all I felt until he should grow stronger, well enough in health for me to handle him as I pleased. But he was snatched away from my madness, to be kept safe with you for my consolation. A few days later, while I was away, the fever returned, and he died.

At this grief the whole of my heart went dark, and everything I looked at was death. My home town was a torment to me, and my father's house a strange misery; and everything I had shared with him became, without him, an excruciating torture. My eyes searched for him everywhere, and he was not given to them; and I hated every place, because none of them held him, nor could any of them say to me now, "Look, he is coming," as they could when he was alive and only away. I had become a great riddle to myself, and I kept asking my soul why it was so downcast and why it disturbed me so. But it had no answer to give me. And if I said, Trust in God, it rightly would not, for the friend it had lost, dear as he was, was a truer and better thing than the phantom it was being told to trust. Only weeping was sweet to me, for it had taken the place of my friend in the dearest of my affections.

And now, Lord, these things are long past, and time has eased my wound. May I learn from you, who are Truth, and bring the ear of my heart close to your mouth, that you may tell me why weeping is sweet to the wretched. Have you, present everywhere, cast our misery far from yourself? You remain at rest in yourself, while we are tossed about from trial to trial. And yet, unless we mourned in your ears, no hope would be left to us. So where does this sweet fruit come from, gathered out of the bitterness of life, out of groaning and tears and sighing and complaint? Is it sweet because we hope you hear us? That is true of prayer, since prayer is a longing to come near you. But is it also true of grief over a thing lost, of the sorrow that overwhelmed me then? For I had no hope he would come back to life, nor was that what my tears asked for; I only wept and grieved. For I was wretched, and I had lost my joy. Or is weeping really a bitter thing after all, sweet to us only in our loathing of the things we used to enjoy, when now we shrink back from them?

But why do I talk of these things? This is no time to ask questions; it is time to confess to you. I was wretched, and wretched is every soul bound fast to things that must perish. It is torn apart when it loses them, and only then feels the wretchedness it was already in before it lost them. So it was then with me. I wept most bitterly, and found my rest in bitterness. So wretched was I that I held that wretched life of mine dearer than my friend. For though I would gladly have changed that life, I was even more unwilling to lose it than to lose him; in fact I do not know whether I would have given it up even for him — as the old story tells (whether true or made up) of Pylades and Orestes, who would gladly have died for each other, or both together, since for them not to live together was worse than death. But some strange feeling had risen in me, the very opposite of theirs: at one and the same time I loathed to be alive and was terrified to die. I suppose the more I loved him, the more I hated and feared, as my cruelest enemy, the death that had robbed me of him; and I imagined that death would suddenly devour all human beings, since it had been able to take him. Yes, that is how it was with me, I remember it. Look into my heart, my God, look and see right into me; for I remember it well, my Hope, you who cleanse me of the filth of such feelings, turning my eyes toward yourself and pulling my feet out of the snare. For I was amazed that other mortals went on living, since the one I had loved as though he would never die was dead; and I was more amazed still that I, who had been a second self to him, could go on living while he was gone. Well did someone say of his friend, "You, the half of my soul" — for I felt that my soul and his had been one soul in two bodies; and so my life was a horror to me, because I would not live as a half. And perhaps that is also why I feared to die: so that he whom I had loved so much would not then be wholly dead.

O madness, that does not know how to love human beings as human beings! O foolish man that I then was, raging against the lot that belongs to every man! So I fretted and sighed and wept; I was torn to pieces; I had neither rest nor good sense. For I was carrying my soul, broken and bleeding, and it could not bear to be carried by me — yet where to set it down, I could not find. Not in cool groves, not in games and song, not in sweet-scented places, not in fine banquets, not in the pleasures of the bed and the couch, not, in the end, in books or in poetry, could it find its rest. Everything was hideous to me, even the light itself; whatever was not what he was, was loathsome and hateful to me — except for groaning and tears, for in those alone I found a little relief. But the moment my soul was drawn away from them, a huge weight of misery pressed me down. To you, Lord, it ought to have been lifted up, for you to lighten; I knew it, but I neither could nor would. The more so since, when I thought of you, you were nothing solid or substantial to me. For it was not you, but an empty phantom, and my error was my god. If I tried to set my load down there for rest, it slid through the emptiness and came rushing back down on me; and I remained to myself an unhappy place where I could neither stay nor leave. For where could my heart flee from my heart? Where could I flee from myself? Where would I not follow myself? And yet I fled my home town, so that my eyes would look for him less in the places where they were not used to seeing him. And so I came from Thagaste to Carthage.

Time takes no time off; it does not roll idly by. Through our senses it works strange changes on the mind. It came and went, day after day, and by its coming and going it planted other imaginings and other memories in me, and little by little patched me up again with the old kinds of delight, before which my grief gave way. Yet what followed was not other griefs, exactly, but the causes of other griefs. For why had that first grief pierced so easily to the very depths of me, except that I had poured out my soul upon the sand, in loving one who must die as though he would never die? What restored and revived me most was the consolation of other friends, with whom I loved what I was loving in the place of you — and this was one great fable, one drawn-out lie, whose adulterous coaxing kept defiling our soul as it lay itching in our ears. Yet that fable did not die in me, however often one of my friends died. There were other things in them that took hold of my mind even more: to talk and laugh together; to do each other kindnesses by turns; to read sweet books together; to fool around together and to be serious together; to disagree at times without any ill will, as a man might with his own self, and by the very rareness of such disagreements to give a flavor to our far more frequent agreements; to teach one another and to learn from one another; to miss the absent with longing, and to welcome them back with joy. By these and the like signs, breaking out of the hearts of those who loved and were loved in return — through the face, the tongue, the eyes, a thousand pleasing gestures — our souls were kindled together as if by so much fuel, and out of many were made one.

This is what is loved in friends, and so loved that a man's own conscience condemns him if he does not love one who loves him back, or does not love in return one who loves him, asking nothing of that other but signs of his love. From this comes the mourning when someone dies, the darkening of sorrows, the heart steeped in tears, all sweetness turned to bitterness; and at the death of the dying, the death of the living. Blessed is the one who loves you, and loves his friend in you, and his enemy for your sake. For he alone loses no one dear to him, to whom all are dear in the One who cannot be lost. And who is that but our God, the God who made heaven and earth and fills them — for by filling them he made them? You no one loses, unless he leaves you. And whoever leaves you, where does he go, where does he flee, but from you in your favor to you in your displeasure? For where does he not run into your law, in his own punishment? And your law is truth, and you are truth.

Turn us back, God of hosts, show us your face, and we shall be whole. For wherever the human soul turns itself, unless it turns toward you, it is nailed fast to sorrows — even when it is nailed to beautiful things. And yet those things, outside you and outside the soul, would not exist at all unless they came from you. They rise and set; by rising, they begin, as it were, to be; they grow toward their fullness, and having reached it they grow old and wither; and not all reach old age, but all wither. So, when they rise and reach toward being, the faster they grow toward being, the faster they hurry toward not-being. This is the law of them. So much you have granted them, because they are parts of things that do not exist all at once, but by passing away and following one another make up the whole universe of which they are the parts. And this is how our own speech is completed by audible signs: it would never be a whole unless each word, having sounded its part, passed away so that another could follow. Let my soul praise you out of all these things, God, Maker of all; but let my soul not be stuck fast to these things by the glue of love, through the body's senses. For they go where they were always going — into not-being — and they tear the soul apart with sick longings, because the soul wants to be, and loves to rest in what it loves. But in these things there is no place of rest, for they do not stay; they flee; and who can follow them with the senses of the flesh? Or who can grasp them even when they are close at hand? For the flesh's sense is slow, because it is the sense of the flesh, and there it has its limit. It is enough for the purpose it was made for, but it is not enough to hold things back as they run their course from their appointed beginning to their appointed end. For in your Word, by which they are created, they hear the decree: "From here, and no farther."

Do not be foolish, my soul, and do not let the ear of your heart be deafened by the uproar of your folly. Listen, you too. The Word itself calls you back; and there is the place of rest that nothing can disturb, where love is not abandoned unless it abandons first. Look — these things pass away so that others may take their place, and so this lower universe may be made complete in all its parts. "But do I go anywhere?" says the Word of God. Fix your dwelling there; entrust to it whatever you have from it, my soul, weary at last as you are of your empty pursuits. Entrust to Truth whatever you have from the Truth, and you will lose nothing; and what has decayed in you will bloom again, and all your sicknesses be healed; what is mortal in you will be made over and made new, bound fast around you. These things will not drag you down with them where they themselves go down; rather, they will stand firm with you and last forever before God, who himself stands firm and lasts forever.

Why, then, be twisted and follow your flesh? Let it instead be turned around and follow you. Whatever you sense through it, you sense only in part; and the whole, of which these are parts, you do not know — and yet they delight you. But if the sense of your flesh were able to take in the whole, and had not, for your punishment, been justly held to a part of the whole, you would wish that whatever exists at this present moment would pass on, so that the whole might please you all the more. For what we speak, you also hear by this same sense of the flesh; yet you would not want the syllables to stand still, but to fly away, so that others may come and you may hear the whole. And so it always is: whenever one thing is made up of many that do not all exist together, all of them together would please more than they do one by one — if only all of them could be taken in together. But far better than all these is the One who made them all; and he is our God, and he does not pass away, for nothing comes after him to take his place.

If bodies please you, praise God on their account, and turn your love back upon their Maker, in case, through the things that please you, you should be displeasing to him. If souls please you, let them be loved in God; for they too are changeable, and only in him are they firmly fixed — otherwise they would pass on and pass away. Let them, then, be loved in him; and carry off to him along with you whatever souls you can, and say to them: "Let us love him, let us love him. He made these things, and he is not far off. For he did not make them and then go away; they come from him and are in him. Look, there he is, wherever truth is loved. He is deep within the heart, but the heart has strayed away from him. Return to your heart, you sinners, and cling fast to him who made you. Stand with him, and you will stand firm. Rest in him, and you will be at rest. Where are you going, by these rough roads? Where are you going? The good that you love is from him; but it is good and pleasant only by reference to him, and justly will it turn bitter, because anything that comes from him is unjustly loved if he is forsaken for it. Why, then, do you keep on walking these hard and weary roads? There is no rest where you are looking for it. Seek what you seek, but it is not there where you seek it. You are looking for a happy life in the land of death; it is not there. For how can there be a happy life where there is no life at all?

"But our true Life came down here, and bore our death, and killed it out of the abundance of his own life. And he thundered, calling out to us to come back from here to him, into that hidden place from which he came out to us — first into the Virgin's womb, where he wedded himself to our human nature, our mortal flesh, so that it would not be mortal forever; and from there, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, he rejoiced as a strong man to run his course. For he did not linger, but ran, calling aloud by words, by deeds, by death, by life, by descent, by ascent, crying out to us to come back to him. And he passed out of our sight, so that we might return into our heart and find him there. For he went away, and look — he is here. He would not stay long with us, and yet he did not leave us; for he went away to the place he had never left, because the world was made through him. He was in this world, and into this world he came to save sinners — to whom my soul confesses, and he heals it, for it has sinned against him. O sons of men, how long will you be so slow of heart? Even now, after Life has come down to you, will you not rise up and live? But where will you climb, when you are already on the heights and have set your mouths against heaven? Come down, so that you may rise — rise up to God. For you fell by trying to climb against him." Tell them this, so that they may weep in the valley of tears, and so carry them up with you to God — because it is out of his Spirit that you speak to them like this, if you speak burning with the fire of love.

These things I did not yet know; I loved those lower beauties, and I was sinking to the very bottom. And I would say to my friends: "Do we love anything but the beautiful? What, then, is the beautiful? And what is beauty? What is it that attracts us and binds us to the things we love? For unless there were a grace and beauty in them, they could never draw us to them at all." And I noticed and worked out that in bodies themselves there is one kind of beauty that comes from a thing's being a whole, and another that comes from a fitting correspondence — as of a part of the body to its whole, or a shoe to a foot, and the like. And this line of thought rose up in my mind out of the depths of my heart, and I wrote a book — two or three books, I think — On the Beautiful and the Fitting. You know, Lord, for it has gone from me; I no longer have it, but it has wandered off, I do not know how.

But what moved me, Lord my God, to dedicate those books to Hierius, an orator of Rome whom I did not know by sight, but loved for the fame of his learning, which was outstanding in him, and for some words of his I had heard, which pleased me? But he pleased me more because he pleased others, who praised him to the skies, marveling that out of a Syrian, first trained in Greek eloquence, there should later have come a wonderful master of Latin and a man deeply learned in matters of philosophy. So a man is praised, and, never seen, is loved. Does this love enter the listener's heart from the mouth of the one who praises? Not at all. Rather, one who loves kindles another. For this is why the man who is praised is loved: when the one praising him is believed to praise him with an honest heart — that is, when the one who praises him truly loves him.

For that is how I loved men in those days, by the judgment of men, not by yours, my God, in whom no one is deceived. But why was it not as one admires a famous charioteer, or a fighter of beasts in the arena, known far and wide by the cheering of the crowd? It was something quite different, and earnest — the way I would have wanted to be admired myself. For I would not have wanted to be praised and loved the way actors are loved, though I myself praised and loved them; I would sooner be unknown than known like that, sooner even hated than loved like that. Where in one soul are all these powers toward so many different and clashing loves stored up? Why do I love in another man — since we are equally men — what, if I did not hate it, I would push away from myself in disgust? It does not hold that, just as a good horse is loved by one who would not want to be that horse even if he could, the same could be said of an actor, who shares our human nature. Do I, then, love in a man what I would hate to be, who am myself a man? Man himself is a great deep, whose very hairs you have numbered, Lord, and they do not fall to the ground without you. And yet the hairs of his head are easier to count than his feelings and the stirrings of his heart.

But that orator was of the kind I loved because I wished to be such a man myself; and I went astray through a swelling pride, tossed about by every wind, and yet steered by you, though very secretly. And how do I know, how do I confess it to you with such confidence, that I had loved him more for the love of those who praised him than for the very things for which he was praised? Because if those same men had run him down instead of praising him, and had told the very same things about him in scorn and contempt, I would never have caught fire and been stirred to love him. And yet the things themselves would have been no different, nor he himself any different — only the feelings of those reporting them. See where the helpless soul lies sprawled, when it is not yet held up by the solidity of truth! Just as the gusts of speech blow from the breasts of people sure of their opinions, the soul is carried this way and that, driven forward and back; the light is overclouded to it, and the truth is not seen — and yet it is right there before us. And it seemed a great thing to me that my work and my labors should be known to that man. If he approved them, I would burn the brighter; but if he disapproved, my empty heart, void of your solid truth, would have been wounded. And yet I dwelt with pleasure on that work On the Beautiful and the Fitting which I wrote to him, and looked it over, and admired it, with no one else to share in it.

But I did not yet see the hinge on which this whole weighty matter turned in your wisdom, almighty one, who alone work wonders. My mind ranged among bodily forms, and I defined and marked off the "beautiful" as what is so in itself, and the "fitting" as what is beautiful in its correspondence to something else; and I backed this up with examples drawn from bodies. I turned to consider the nature of the mind, but the false notion I had of spiritual things would not let me see the truth. And yet the very force of truth flashed before my eyes, and I turned my panting soul away from bodiless reality toward shapes and colors and swelling bulks; and because I could not see these in the mind, I thought I could not see my mind. And whereas I loved peace in virtue and hated discord in vice, in the one I noticed a unity, and in the other a kind of division. And in that unity I imagined the rational soul to lie, and the nature of truth and of the highest good; while in that division I wretchedly imagined there to be some substance of irrational life, and the very nature of the highest evil — which I took to be not only a substance but a real life of its own, and yet not derived from you, my God, from whom all things come. And the first of these I called a Monad, as if it were a soul without sex; the second a Duad — anger in deeds of violence, and lust in shameful acts — not knowing what I was talking about. For I had neither known nor learned that evil is not a substance at all, nor that our soul is not that highest and unchangeable good.

For just as deeds of violence arise when the impulse of the soul is corrupted from which vehement action springs, when it stirs itself up insolently and out of control; and lusts arise when that affection of the soul is ungoverned by which bodily pleasures are drunk in — so do errors and false opinions defile the way one lives, when the reasonable soul itself is corrupted. So it was then in me, who did not know that it must be lit by another light if it is to share in the truth, since it is not itself the nature of truth. For you will light my lamp, Lord my God; you will brighten my darkness; and of your fullness we have all received, for you are the true light that lights every man coming into the world — for in you there is no change, nor any shadow of turning.

But I was pressing toward you, and was thrust back from you, so that I might taste death; for you resist the proud. And what was prouder than for me, in a strange madness, to claim that I was by nature what you are? For though I was subject to change — and that much was plain to me, since my very wish to grow wise was the wish to become better out of worse — I chose instead to imagine you subject to change, rather than admit that I was not what you are. So I was driven back, and you stood against my empty stubbornness; and I went on imagining bodily forms, and, being flesh myself, I accused flesh; and, a wind that passes and does not return, I did not turn back to you, but passed on and on toward things that have no being at all — neither in you, nor in me, nor in any body — things not created for me by your truth, but invented out of bodily things by my own emptiness. And I used to ask your faithful little ones — my fellow citizens, from whom, without knowing it, I stood exiled — I used to ask them, prattling and foolish: "Why, then, does the soul go astray, when God created it?" But I would not let myself be asked, "Why, then, does God go astray?" And I would maintain that your unchangeable substance went astray under compulsion, rather than confess that my own changeable substance had gone astray of its own free will, and now, in punishment, lay in error.

I was about twenty-six or twenty-seven when I wrote those books, turning over inside me those bodily fictions that buzzed in the ears of my heart — that heart which I was straining, sweet Truth, toward your inward music, meditating on the "beautiful and the fitting," longing to stand still and listen to you and rejoice greatly at the Bridegroom's voice; but I could not, for by the voices of my own errors I was hurried away outside, and by the weight of my own pride I was sinking into the lowest pit. For you had not yet made me to hear joy and gladness, nor did the bones rejoice that had not yet been humbled.

And what did it profit me that, when I was scarcely twenty, a book of Aristotle's that they call the Ten Categories fell into my hands — at whose very name I hung as on something great and divine, every time my teacher of rhetoric at Carthage and others reckoned learned would mouth it with cheeks bursting with pride — and I read it and understood it on my own, with no help? When I compared notes with others, who said they had barely understood it even with very able teachers, who not only explained it aloud but drew many diagrams in the sand, they could tell me no more about it than I had learned reading it by myself. And the book seemed to me to speak quite clearly of substances, such as "man," and of their qualities — the shape of a man, what sort it is; his height, how many feet tall; his kinship, whose brother he is; where he is placed; when he was born; whether he is standing or sitting; whether he is shod or armed; whether he is doing something or having something done to him — and of all the countless things that can be ranged under those nine categories, of which I have given a few samples, or under that chief category of Substance.

What did all this advance me — when in fact it held me back? For, imagining that whatever exists is taken in under those ten categories, I tried in the same way to understand your own wonderful and unchangeable Oneness, my God — as if you too were laid out under your own greatness or beauty, so that they should exist in you as their subject, the way they do in bodies; whereas you yourself are your own greatness and beauty, while a body is not great or beautiful by being a body, since even if it were less great or beautiful it would still be a body. For what I thought of you was falsehood, not truth — the fictions of my misery, not the realities of your blessedness. For you had commanded, and it was done in me, that the earth should bring forth thorns and briars for me, and that with the sweat of my brow I should eat my bread.

And what did it profit me that all the books I could get hold of on what they call the liberal arts, I — the vile slave of vile desires — read and understood by myself? I took delight in them, but I did not know where all that was true or certain in them came from. For I had my back to the light and my face to the things lit by it; so that my face, with which I looked at the things lit, was not itself lit. Whatever was written on rhetoric or logic, on geometry, music, and arithmetic, I understood, you know it, Lord my God, without much trouble and with no instructor — for both quickness of understanding and sharpness of discernment are your gift. But for this I offered no sacrifice to you. So it served not my benefit but my ruin, since I was trying to get so good a portion of my substance into my own keeping; and I did not keep my strength for you, but wandered away from you into a far country, to squander it on harlotries. For what did good abilities profit me, if I did not put them to good use? For I did not feel how hard those arts were to master, even for the diligent and gifted, until I tried to explain them to such people — and the best among them was the one who could keep up with me without falling too far behind.

But what did this advance me, while I imagined that you, Lord God, the Truth, were a vast and shining body, and I a fragment of that body? Perverseness too great! But that is what I was. And I do not blush, my God, to confess to you your mercies toward me, and to call upon you — I who did not blush then to profess my blasphemies to men, and to bark against you. What good to me then was my nimble wit in those studies, all those most knotty books unraveled by me without any help of human teaching, when in the teaching of true devotion I went so foully and sacrilegiously astray? And what harm was a far slower wit to your little ones, since they did not depart far from you, but in the nest of your Church grew their feathers in safety, and nourished the wings of love on the food of a sound faith? Lord our God, let us hope under the shadow of your wings; protect us and carry us. You will carry us — you will carry us when we are small, and even to gray hairs you will carry us. For when our firmness is you, then it is firmness; but when it is our own, it is weakness. Our good lives forever with you, and when we turn away from it, we are turned aside. Let us now return, Lord, so that we are not overturned, since with you our good lives on without any decay — and that good is you. And we need not fear that there is no place to return to, just because we fell from it; for in our absence our home did not fall — your eternity.

Accept the sacrifice of my confessions from the labor of my tongue, which you yourself shaped and stirred up to confess to your name. Heal all my bones, and let them say, Lord, who is like you? For the one who confesses to you is not teaching you what goes on inside him; a closed heart does not shut out your eye, and a man's hardness cannot push back your hand. You dissolve that hardness whenever you please, in pity or in punishment, and nothing can hide itself from your heat. But let my soul praise you, so that it may love you; let it confess your own mercies to you, so that it may praise you. Your whole creation never stops, never falls silent in your praises — not the spirit of a man whose voice is turned toward you, nor anything alive or lifeless, by the voice of those who consider it — so that our souls may rise up out of their weariness toward you, leaning on the things you have made and passing on through them to you, who made them so wonderfully. There is refreshment, and there is the true strength.

Let the restless and the godless leave you and run; still you see them and divide the darkness. And look — with them in it, the universe is beautiful, though they themselves are foul. How have they hurt you? How have they disgraced your rule, which from the heavens down to this lowest earth is just and complete? Where did they flee to, when they fled from your presence? Where would you not find them? They fled so as not to see you seeing them, and, blinded, stumble against you — for you forsake nothing you have made. They stumble against you, the unjust, and are justly hurt: drawing back from your gentleness, tripping over your uprightness, falling on their own roughness. They do not know, in truth, that you are everywhere, that no place can hold you, and that you alone are near even to those who take themselves far from you. So let them turn and look for you. For you have not forsaken your creation the way they have forsaken their Creator. Let them turn and look for you, and there you are, in their heart — in the heart of those who confess to you and throw themselves on you and weep on your breast after all their rugged ways. Gently you wipe away their tears, and they weep the more, and rejoice in their weeping; because you, Lord — not some man of flesh and blood, but you, Lord, who made them — remake them and comfort them. And where was I, when I was looking for you? You were there in front of me, but I had gone away from myself, and could not even find myself, much less you.

Let me lay open before my God that twenty-ninth year of my life. There had come to Carthage by then a certain bishop of the Manichees, Faustus by name, a great snare of the devil, and many were caught in it by the bait of his smooth tongue. I admired that tongue myself, and yet I could tell it apart from the truth of the things I was so eager to learn. It was not the serving-dish of his rhetoric I cared about, but the knowledge that this Faustus, so famous among them, was supposed to set before me to feed on. Rumor had run ahead of him: he was a master of every worthwhile study, deeply skilled in the liberal arts. And since I had read a good deal of the philosophers, and kept it well, I held some of their findings up against the long fables of the Manichees, and found the philosophers more believable — even though their reach went only so far as to take the measure of this lower world; the Lord of that world they could not find at all. For you are great, Lord, and you look on the lowly, but the proud you see only from far off. You come near to none but the contrite in heart; the proud do not find you, not even if by some clever skill they could count the stars and the sands, chart the shining heavens, and trace the courses of the planets.

With the mind and wit you gave them they search these things out, and much they have discovered: they foretold eclipses of those great lights, the sun and moon, years ahead — the very day, the hour, how far the shadow would reach — and their reckoning did not fail; it happened just as they said. They wrote down the rules they had worked out, and those rules are read to this day, and from them others foretell in what year and month, on what day and at what hour, and to what depth, the sun or moon will be darkened, and so it comes to pass exactly as foreshown. People who do not know this art are astonished and amazed; those who do know it crow and swell with pride. For by a godless pride they slip away from you and lose your light: they foresee, so long beforehand, a coming failure of the sun's light, and cannot see the failure of their own, here and now. They make no reverent search into where they got the very wit they search with. And when they find that you made them, they do not hand themselves over to you to keep what you made; they do not put to death, as a sacrifice to you, the selves they have made of themselves. They do not slaughter their own soaring presumptions, like birds of the air, nor their prying curiosities, by which, like the fish of the sea, they wander the trackless deep, nor their own self-indulgence, like the beasts of the field — so that you, Lord, a devouring fire, might burn up those dead concerns of theirs and remake the men themselves for life that does not end.

But they did not know the way, your Word, by whom you made the very things they count, and the counters themselves, and the sense by which they perceive what they count, and the understanding out of which they count — for of your wisdom there is no number. Yet the Only-Begotten was made, for us, wisdom and righteousness and holiness, and was counted among us, and paid his tax to Caesar. They did not know this way, by which to climb down from themselves to him and by him climb up to him. They did not know it, and reckoned themselves high among the stars and shining; and look — they fell to earth, and their foolish heart was darkened. They say many true things about the creation, but the Truth who crafted the creation they do not look for in the right spirit, and so do not find — or if they do find him, and know him to be God, they do not honor him as God, nor give thanks, but lose themselves in their own notions, and call themselves wise, claiming for their own what is yours. And so, with the most twisted blindness, they go on to charge you with what is theirs, telling lies about you who are the Truth, trading the glory of the incorruptible God for an image made like corruptible man, and birds, and beasts, and crawling things — swapping your truth for a lie, and worshiping and serving the creature in place of the Creator.

Even so, I held on to many true things about the created world that I had from these men, and I saw the reason of them in the calculations, the succession of seasons, and the visible witness of the stars. I set them beside the sayings of Manichaeus, who in his ravings had written at huge length on these very subjects, and I could find in him no account of the solstices, or the equinoxes, or the eclipses of the greater lights, nor anything of the kind I had learned in the books of ordinary philosophy. Yet I was ordered to believe him — and it did not square with what calculation and my own eyes had settled; it ran flat against them.

Does anyone, then, Lord God of truth, please you just because he knows these things? Surely the man who knows all of that and does not know you is wretched, and the man who knows you, even if he knows none of it, is happy. And the man who knows both you and them is no happier for knowing them, but happy in you alone — if, knowing you, he glorifies you as God, and gives thanks, and does not lose himself in his own notions. For just as a man is better off who knows how to own a tree and thank you for the use of it, though he cannot say how many feet high it stands or how wide it spreads, than one who can measure it and count every branch but neither owns it nor knows and loves the One who made it — so a believer, to whom all this wealth of a world belongs, who having nothing yet possesses all things by clinging to you, whom all things serve, even if he does not know so much as the turning of the Great Bear, it is folly to doubt that he is better off than the man who can measure the sky and number the stars and weigh the elements, yet has no thought for you, who made all things in number and weight and measure.

But still — who told that Manichaeus to write on these matters too, when skill in them is no part of devotion? For you have said to man, Behold, devotion and wisdom are this. Of astronomy he might have been ignorant and still had wisdom; but these things, of which he knew nothing, he shamelessly dared to teach, and so plainly could have no knowledge of devotion. For to make a show of these worldly matters, even when you do know them, is vanity; but to confess to you is devotion. That is why this wanderer talked so much about them: so that, once he was caught out by people who had truly learned them, it would be clear how little understanding he had in the deeper, more hidden things. For he would not be thought a small man; he went about persuading people that the Holy Spirit, the Comforter and Enricher of your faithful, was present in his own person, with full authority. So when he was caught teaching falsely about the heavens and the stars and the movements of sun and moon — though such things have nothing to do with the teaching of religion — even so his blasphemous nerve stood exposed, since he handed out things he not only did not know but had got plainly wrong, and with such a mad swollen pride that he tried to ascribe them to himself, as to a divine person.

For when I hear some Christian brother who knows nothing of these matters and has them confused, I can look on his mistakes with patience; I do not see how any ignorance about the place or make-up of the physical world can harm him, as long as he believes nothing unworthy of you, Lord, the Creator of all. It does harm him if he takes such things to belong to the body of devout teaching, and stubbornly insists on what he does not know. Yet even such a weakness, in the infancy of faith, our mother Charity carries, until the newborn grows up to a full-grown man, no longer blown about by every wind of doctrine. But in a man who set himself up as the teacher, the source, the guide, the head of all he could persuade — so that whoever followed him thought he was following not a mere man but your Holy Spirit — who would not judge that so vast a madness, once caught teaching anything false, was to be loathed and utterly thrown off? Still, I had not yet made out for certain whether the changing lengths of days and nights, and of day and night themselves, and the eclipses of the greater lights, and whatever else of the kind I had read of, could be squared with his sayings; so that, if they somehow could, it would still be an open question to me whether it was so or not, and I might rest my belief on his authority for the sake of his supposed holiness.

And for nearly all those nine years in which, with an unsettled mind, I had been their student, I had been longing for the coming of this Faustus, too intensely. For the others of the sect, the ones I happened to fall in with, when they could not answer my questions about these things, kept holding out this Faustus to me, by whose coming and by talking with whom these difficulties and any greater ones would be cleared up most easily and fully. So when he came, I found a man of pleasant conversation, who said the very same things they all said, but in better and smoother words. But what good was the most elegant cupbearer to a thirst that wanted a more precious drink? My ears were already glutted with all this, and it did not seem any better to me for being better said, nor true for being eloquent, nor the soul wise because the face was handsome and the speech well-turned. But those who held him out to me were no judges of such things, and so to them he seemed thoughtful and wise, because he was pleasant to listen to. I had noticed, though, that there are people who grow suspicious even of the truth, and will not give their assent to it, if it is delivered in a smooth and copious style. But you, my God, had already taught me by wonderful, hidden ways — and I believe it was you who taught me, because it is true, and there is no teacher of truth but you, wherever and from wherever it may shine on us. So from you I had already learned that nothing should seem true just because it is well said, nor false because the words come out rough; nor, again, true because plainly put, nor false because richly worded. Wisdom and folly are like wholesome and unwholesome food, and polished or plain phrases are like fine or common dishes: either kind of food may be served in either kind of dish.

So the hunger with which I had waited so long for that man was delighted, true enough, by his energy and warmth in debate, and by the apt, ready words he found to dress his ideas. I was delighted, and along with many others — more than they — I praised and exalted him. It troubled me, though, that in the crowd around him I could never get my turn to bring forward the questions that were troubling me, in a real exchange with him. When at last I could, and began with my friends to engage his attention at times when it was not unfitting for him to talk it over with me, and laid before him the things that moved me, I found him first of all ignorant of the liberal arts, except for grammar, and that only in an ordinary way. But because he had read a few of Cicero's speeches, a very few books of Seneca, some of the poets, and the handful of his own sect's volumes that were written in good Latin, and because he practiced speaking every day, he had picked up a certain eloquence, the more pleasing and seductive for being guided by a good wit and a kind of natural grace. Is it not so, as I recall it, Lord my God, judge of my conscience? Before you lie my heart and my memory — you who were guiding me even then by the hidden working of your providence, and setting those shameful errors of mine before my face, that I might see them and hate them.

For once it was clear that he knew nothing of the arts I had thought him a master of, I began to despair of his opening up and solving the difficulties that perplexed me — though, ignorant of all that as he was, he might still have held the truths of devotion, had he not been a Manichee. Their books are stuffed with long-winded fables about the heavens, the stars, the sun and moon; and I no longer thought him able to settle what I so badly wanted settled: whether, when these things were set against the calculations I had read elsewhere, the account in the books of Manichaeus was the better, or at least as good. When I put this up to be weighed and discussed, he, modestly enough, shrank from the load. He knew that he did not know these things, and was not ashamed to admit it. For he was not one of those many talkers I had put up with, who undertook to teach me these matters and said nothing. This man had a heart, not right toward you, and yet not altogether false to himself: he was not wholly ignorant of his own ignorance, and would not rashly let himself be drawn into an argument from which he could find no honest retreat or way out. And for that I liked him the better. For the modesty of a candid mind is a fairer thing than the very knowledge I was after — and that is how I found him in all the harder and subtler questions.

With my zeal for the writings of Manichaeus thus blunted, and despairing all the more of their other teachers now that the famous one had turned out so, I began to spend my time with him in the study of literature, which he too was keen on — and which, as a teacher of rhetoric, I was then teaching young men at Carthage — reading with him either what he wanted to hear or what I judged suited to his talent. But all the efforts by which I had meant to advance in that sect came utterly to an end once I knew the man — not that I broke with them altogether, but, finding nothing better, I had settled to make do for the time with whatever I had stumbled into, unless by chance something more worth choosing should dawn on me. So that Faustus, who to so many had been a snare of death, had now, without willing or even knowing it, begun to loosen the snare that held me. For your hands, my God, in the secret purpose of your providence, did not let go of my soul; and out of the blood of my mother's heart, through her tears poured out for me day and night, a sacrifice was being offered to you on my behalf, and you dealt with me in wonderful ways. You did it, my God — for a man's steps are ordered by the Lord, and he shall direct his way. And how else are we to find salvation, except from your hand, remaking what it made?

You dealt with me, then, so that I was talked into going to Rome, to teach there what I was teaching at Carthage.
